models.summary: Equity from the New Palgrave no-envy definition, mapped from persons to countries. Population-weighted Theil index, then a log correction so population size does not dominate. National power is a three-factor score on 12 indicators for 8 countries; grades A-D feed the Theil index. Gini 0.4-0.44 is the cross-check.
models.purpose: Measure international inequity as a decomposable Theil index of national power.
objectives: Replace personal income with national power inside a population-weighted, log-corrected Theil index.

parameter_estimation.method: Factor analysis in SAS. Keep the first three factors once cumulative contribution exceeds 80 percent.

algorithm.description: Map persons to countries, reject the unweighted Theil by reductio, weight by population, log-correct, score national power by factor analysis, grade A-D, plot Theil over time, cross-check with Gini.
algorithm.convergence_criteria: First three factors exceed 80 percent of variance.

details: United States score 0.953, China 0.452, India 0.712 in the 2017 table as printed. World Gini stays between 0.4 and 0.44.
identifiability_feasibility.analysis: A-with-D pairing produces a large Theil index, which the authors treat as a reality check.

strengths: Decomposability is the reason the index is chosen, not a decoration.
The Vatican reductio kills the unweighted form in one sentence.
limitations: Eight countries cannot carry a world equity claim.
The log correction's exact algebra is not recoverable from the OCR.
missing_details: Exact printed forms of equations (1), (2), and (3).
assumptions: National power can stand in for personal income.
A short modern window has roughly constant conditions.

models.summary: n mining-capable countries treated as firms. Cooperative-competition equilibrium payoff exceeds the Nash payoff of full competition and is judged more realistic than full cooperation. Pioneers therefore move from competition to cooperation. A one-country Lucky shock (+15 percent GDP in 2005) then spikes the Theil index between mining and non-mining countries.
models.purpose: Show why mining pioneers cooperate, and why that cooperation still widens the gap with everyone else.
objectives: Compare cooperative-competition profit with Nash profit, then show the equity cost for non-mining countries.

Equilibrium profit under full Nash competition
GDP increase of the single mining country, set to 0.15 for Lucky
Theil index between mining and non-mining countries after the shock

algorithm.description: Solve the n-country game, compare payoffs, conclude cooperation, then apply the Lucky shock and plot three Theil curves.

details: Prose says cooperative benefits exceed competitive benefits. The yes-no Theil curve jumps after 2005.
identifiability_feasibility.analysis: Cooperation is privately rational and globally unequal. That tension is the paper's real result.

validation_refs: Figure 10 Change in Theil index before and after Lucky
strengths: The one-line pivot 'Is this the end?' separates the private win from the global loss.
A named hypothetical makes the shock readable.
limitations: 15 percent is an unmotivated round number.
assumptions: Capable countries stay fixed in the short run.

models.summary: Multi-objective Shapley allocation of Lucky2. Monte Carlo heat map peaks at row 30, column 30; scaled Shapley values 0.6437 for mining-capable countries and 0.5982 for the others. Post-cooperation Theil falls. Lucky3 adds 0.05 to every indicator; path coefficients 0.45, 0.38, 0.29 run through GDP, trade, and income per capita. Three historical shocks: technological rise, resource curse, interest-group relapse.
models.purpose: Allocate mining gains so equity improves, then say which economic channels carry the effect.
objectives: Maximize cooperative gain subject to a floor, then attribute the equity effect to three economic paths.

details: Discovery and cooperation both set to 2005. Lucky3 mined in the earlier sample countries.
More-work-more-pay, with a tilt toward countries in need.

parameter_estimation.method: Monte Carlo over contribution pairs; path coefficients from the linear system after the simulated lift.

algorithm.description: Build a multi-objective Shapley game, scan contribution pairs by Monte Carlo, allocate at the heat-map peak, recompute Theil, then run path analysis under Lucky3 and three historical scenarios.
algorithm.convergence_criteria: Heat-map cell with the largest revenue.

details: 0.6437 and 0.5982. Path coefficients 0.45, 0.38, 0.29. Theil falls after cooperation and rebounds under the resource curse and under monopoly relapse.
identifiability_feasibility.analysis: The allocation result is the paper's policy number. The path result says the channel is the economy, not technology or territory.

constraints: Labor-based distribution as the main rule.
strengths: One heat-map cell is a clearer optimum than a verbal 'balance'.
Historical analogues (France 1870-1897, OPEC) keep the scenarios from being free invention.
limitations: Row 30 and column 30 are not defined in units of contribution.
Monte Carlo repeated use weakens generality, as the authors admit.
missing_details: Axis scaling of the heat map.
assumptions: Cooperation yields more than separate mining.
A flat indicator lift can stand in for an unknown mineral.
